items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: I knew him quite well because they used to come through Columbus, Ohio.

ctx.x: You know, I never saw the connection.

Oh, we worked together around St. Louis a long time, Jo Jones and I. And Walter Page. And then a trumpet player, a tenor player, they added another tenor player to the band which is Gene Porter. He used to play with Earl Hines and then they had a band there who I just read in this book that they connected me with, Eddie Johnson and his Cracker Jacks. Harold Baker was playing with that band, see, and I never did play with the band. But I knew him quite well because they used to come through Columbus, Ohio. That's…

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Lucky Millinder sent for Hal Baker and a tenor saxophone player from Cleveland named Harold Arnold.

ctx.x: Was he soloing like he eventually did with Duke?

Oh yeah, he was soloing then, he was soloing while the band was playing. But he soloed in a way that he still was swinging. And he was just with Jeter-Pillars for a short time. Then Ellington came through there and snatched him away. At that time the big band used to come through St. Louis all the time, they were taking everybody. Later on, they got Harold Baker, Shorty Baker. He went with Don Redman first, then he went with Ellington. That’s the way I got to New York, really. It was really funny how I got to New…
But you didn’t try and go under the name of Harold Baker.

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: All those people like Shorty Baker and poor Taft, he's very well.

ctx.x: The third set of the night, he's doing right. But you've really -- you're almost the exception there. All those people like Shorty Baker and poor Taft, he's very well. Doc Cheatham is about the only other one.
Yeah, he's in his late 70's, too.
